t: Listen to a talk in a philosophy class.
Today, we're going to explore the concept of existentialism, a philosophical movement that emerged in the twentieth century.
A central concept in existentialism is the absurd, a term popularized by Albert Camus.
It describes the conflict between our deep desire for meaning and the indifferent, chaotic nature of the universe.
Camus argued that while life may lack inherent purpose, we must still live with integrity and passion, embracing the absurd rather than succumbing to despair.
This theme is powerfully explored in Samuel Beckett's play Waiting for Godot.
Two characters, Vladimir and Estragon, wait endlessly for someone named Godot, who never arrives.
Their repetitive conversations and actions highlight the emptiness and uncertainty of existence.
Rather than dramatic expressions of anxiety, the play presents a quieter, more subdued response to the absurd, one marked by endurance and the faint hope that meaning might eventually appear.
One anecdote suggests Beckett was inspired by a story about a man actually waiting for someone named Godot who never came.
When asked who Godot was, Beckett famously replied, If I knew, I would have said so in the play.
This ambiguity is part of what makes the work so powerful.
It captures existentialism not through answers but through the act of questioning and enduring.
